chunks: Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn, from Safwan, from Isḥāq ibn ʿAmmār, who said:

I said to Abū Ibrāhīm (peace be upon him): 'For the absent husband whose wife is divorced, what is the duration of his absence?' He said: 'Five months or six months.' I said: 'What is the minimum limit below that?' He said: 'Three months.' Because the way to reconcile between these two reports and the first report is to say: 'The ruling varies according to the custom of women regarding menstruation. So whoever knows of his wife's condition that she menstruates once every month, it is permissible for him to divorce her after the month ends. And whoever knows that she does not menstruate except every three months or five months, it is not permissible for him to divorce her except after the passage of this period.' Thus, the consideration in the permissibility of that is the passage of one menstruation and its transition to a period of purity in which he did not have intercourse with her, and that varies according to what we have said.
ai.seo_question: What is the waiting period for divorcing an absent husband's wife according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Isfabar elucidates the concept of 'Iddah al-Gha'ib' (waiting period for an absent husband), where Imam al-Baqir (AS) establishes that the duration is determined by the wife's habitual menstrual cycle rather than a fixed calendar count. This ruling highlights the Shia jurisprudential principle of 'Urf' (customary practice) in determining legal obligations, ensuring the waiting period aligns with the biological reality of the individual woman. It serves as a practical application of Quranic verses on divorce, bridging divine law with observable human nature.
